title: The Breaking Point
teaser: The eye is sliced, the markets collapse, rationality declares victory. In a single year, surrealism invades cinema, modernism invades the museum, and Wall Street proves that collective madness has nothing to do with reason. Philosophy debates whether human finitude or symbolic infinity defines us—while the answer arrives on Black Tuesday.

art.label: Art
art.content: Un Chien Andalou premieres in Paris on June sixth—Surrealism's most notorious assault on bourgeois perception. Luis Buñuel and Salvador Dalí construct their screenplay from pure dream logic: a razor slices an eye, ants crawl from a palm, dead donkeys drape across pianos. The Surrealist movement, born from Dada's nihilism but seeking the unconscious rather than mere destruction, finds its perfect medium in cinema. Meanwhile in New York, the Museum of Modern Art opens on November seventh—just nine days after Black Tuesday. Three visionary patrons (Abby Aldrich Rockefeller, Lillie P. Bliss, Mary Quinn Sullivan) institutionalize the avant-garde, declaring that modern art deserves the same curatorial seriousness as the Old Masters.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: William Faulkner publishes The Sound and the Fury, literary modernism's most radical American experiment. Four narrators, three of them unreliable—including Benjy, whose section fragments time into pure sensation. The title quotes Macbeth: life as 'a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing.' Hemingway's A Farewell to Arms appears the same year, but where Faulkner dissolves consciousness, Hemingway strips it to bone. Both respond to the war's destruction of nineteenth-century certainties, but through opposite techniques: maximum interiority versus maximum restraint.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: In March, Heidegger and Cassirer meet at Davos for the century's defining philosophical debate. Cassirer defends Neo-Kantianism: humanity transcends finitude through symbolic forms—language, myth, science—reaching toward objective truth. Heidegger counters that Dasein is fundamentally finite, thrown into time, facing death. In September, the Vienna Circle publishes its manifesto, The Scientific Conception of the World: all meaningful statements are either empirically verifiable or logically analytic. Metaphysics is literally nonsense. Two visions of reason clash: one embracing anxiety and mortality, one demanding scientific precision.

hist.label: History
hist.content: On Black Thursday (October twenty-fourth), panic selling hits the New York Stock Exchange. On Black Tuesday (October twenty-ninth), sixteen million shares trade—the ticker tape runs hours behind reality as fortunes evaporate. The Dow will eventually lose eighty-nine percent of its value. The Roaring Twenties' speculative mania—margin buying, irrational exuberance—collapses into the Great Depression. Fourteen billion dollars vanishes in a single day. The crash exposes the gap between market confidence and economic fundamentals, triggering a decade of global catastrophe.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The year's convergence is reason against unreason—or their strange complicity. The Vienna Circle declares that only verifiable statements have meaning; Dalí and Buñuel insist that dreams reveal truths logic cannot reach. Heidegger argues that authentic existence requires confronting mortality; Wall Street discovers that collective behavior can be as irrational as any nightmare. MoMA opens amid ruins, betting that art matters more when everything else fails. Faulkner's idiot narrator and the Vienna Circle's logical syntax are mirror images: both strip language to its limits, one through reduction to sense-data, the other through dissolution into consciousness.
conn.funFact: Buñuel attended Un Chien Andalou's premiere with stones in his pockets, ready to throw at the audience if they attacked—but the Surrealists cheered instead.
